meta.description: Narrowly-scoped, claim-matched external reference registry for wine-fault scientific/domain claims only. This is NOT the same structure as data/relationship-evidence.json — that file's 'evidence' field is internal reasoning support for the site's own relationship graph. This file holds independently-verified EXTERNAL sources, deliberately named to avoid that terminology collision (per PAIRING-EAT-09's explicit finding). Never attach a record here to Pairing Strength, wine rankings, or any Pairing Method editorial/model output — only to the specific general-domain scientific/technical claim named in claims_supported.

sources.source_type: professional oenology research institute — technical reference

claims_supported.exact_claim_text: Chlorophenols from sanitizers, wood treatments, or environmental exposure convert to TCA via fungal metabolism. The compound transfers to wine at parts-per-trillion thresholds through cork contact or cellar contamination.
claims_supported.why_source_supports_claim: AWRI's page states, on direct verification: 'TCA is generally formed as a result of moulds growing on cork and coming into contact with trichlorophenol... Some moulds can detoxify the trichlorophenol and related chlorophenols by adding a methyl group to the benzene ring to form TCA' — directly confirming the chlorophenol-to-TCA fungal/mould conversion mechanism. It also confirms 'TCA can be formed in oak, and as a result wines can have a TCA taint without any contact with cork,' supporting the claim that transfer occurs via non-cork contamination routes as well. The page does not independently confirm the specific 'parts-per-trillion' threshold figure or 'packaging materials' as a source — the citation is scoped to the chlorophenol/fungal-conversion mechanism only, not every clause in the paragraph.

claims_supported.exact_claim_text: Spoilage yeast (Brettanomyces bruxellensis and related strains) metabolizing hydroxycinnamic acids into volatile phenols.
claims_supported.why_source_supports_claim: AWRI's FAQ states, on direct verification: 'Brettanomyces ("Brett") is a type of yeast commonly found in wineries, which has the potential to cause significant spoilage in wines, through the production of volatile phenol compounds' and '4-EP and 4-EG, the two main compounds associated with "Brett", originate from two hydroxycinnamic acid precursors: p-coumaric and ferulic acids' — directly confirming the spoilage-yeast-to-volatile-phenol-via-hydroxycinnamic-acid mechanism. CAVEAT recorded honestly: this AWRI page uses the genus-level term 'Brettanomyces' throughout and does not itself name the species 'bruxellensis' specifically. Brettanomyces bruxellensis is the standard, uncontroversial species identification in the wine-spoilage literature (corroborated by independent search results naming it directly, e.g. peer-reviewed titles referencing 'Brettanomyces bruxellensis phenotypic diversity' and 'Dekkera/Brettanomyces bruxellensis'), but this specific citation is scoped to the mechanism/sensory-outcome claim, not to the species-name detail.
